food.name: Flax Seeds

identity.basisReason: The raw whole-seed per-100g identity is the canonical whole-food comparison entry; grinding is treated as preparation guidance rather than a separate food variant.
includes: ground flax prepared from the same whole seed
excludes: defatted flax meal or protein isolate

scoreReadiness.summary: Complete per-100g raw flaxseed profile with exact USDA nutrients and amino acids, a clearly labelled human digestibility proxy, and source-backed context.
caveats: The protein-digestibility measurement used an isolate baked into biscuits rather than intact raw whole seeds.
The glycemic-index value is a contextual estimate rather than a direct universal laboratory value for intact whole flaxseed.
Cultivar, storage, grinding, and preparation can change the realised nutrient access from flaxseed.

sourceNotes: Production-safe raw whole-food entry scored per 100g.
USDA SR Legacy FDC 169414 supplies the canonical nutrient and amino-acid profile.

The 92.2% protein-digestibility value is a human true-ileal measurement of flaxseed protein isolate incorporated into biscuits, so the processed-isolate-to-whole-seed form mismatch is preserved in provenance.
Protein digestibility means digested and absorbed, making amino acids available for use; it is not the same as the study's separate 71.3% net postprandial protein-utilisation result.

topPros.title: one of the richest lignan food sources
topPros.explanation: Flax is unusually concentrated in plant lignans, which gut microbes can convert into enterolignans.

topPros.title: ground seed works as an egg-free binder
topPros.explanation: Mixed with water, ground flax forms a gel that can bind simple batters and bakes.

topPros.title: easy shelf-stable meal add-on
topPros.explanation: Ground flax can disappear into oats, yogurt, smoothies, and dough without needing a separate meal.

topCons.title: whole seeds leave more nutrition locked away
topCons.explanation: Human crossover research found milling substantially improved access to flax lignans compared with intact seeds.

topCons.title: large amounts can feel rough
topCons.explanation: Large amounts can cause bloating, fullness, or diarrhoea, especially when intake rises quickly.

topCons.title: 100g is far beyond a normal serving
topCons.explanation: The comparison basis is useful for ranking, but a spoonful delivers only a fraction of the displayed totals.

closing.summary: Best bits are the massive ALA omega 3 mark, extreme fibre, useful protein, magnesium, and the lignan story. Weak spots are the thin vitamin panel, limited lysine, lower payoff from swallowing the seeds whole, and digestive tolerance. Best for heart-health-focused meals, digestion, and easy meal upgrades because the fats and fibre are genuinely strong and ground flax is simple to use. This is one of the clearest seed-category wins.

scenes.narrationText: 42.2 grams of fat. Omega 3 is an enormous 22813 milligrams, almost all ALA, the plant form your body can use directly and convert in small amounts into longer-chain omega 3s. Saturated fat is only 3.7 grams, keeping the fat tradeoff unusually clean. For seeds, fat quality is one of the main jobs, and flax absolutely nails it.

scenes.narrationText: 18.3 grams of protein. Essential amino acids score is 9 out of 9, so every essential group clears FoodRanked's useful-amount threshold. Nonessential amino acids score 9 out of 11, still strong but the softer mark. Protein digestibility is about 92%, meaning most of that protein can be digested and absorbed, making its amino acids available for the body to use. Lysine is still the limiting amino acid, so highly digestible does not mean perfectly balanced. For seeds, that makes flax strong support protein rather than a perfect standalone source.

scenes.narrationText: Vitamins are low all round. Vitamin K is the best mark at only 4% daily value, while vitamin E is 2%. Vitamin K supports normal blood clotting and bone proteins, and vitamin E helps protect cell membranes, but these amounts are tiny. Seeds usually win through fats, fibre, and minerals, and flax is no exception.

scenes.narrationText: The upsides first: one of the richest everyday lignan sources. Lignans are plant compounds that gut bacteria can turn into enterolignans, giving flax a named-compound story beyond the visible nutrient rows. Grinds into an egg-free baking binder. Mix ground flax with water and it forms a gel that can help bind pancakes, muffins, and other bakes. Cheap and shelf-stable whole. The intact seeds keep well and are easy to add to porridge, yoghurt, or dough without a full recipe.

scenes.narrationText: The drawbacks next: whole seeds can pass through partly undigested. Human research found much better lignan availability after crushing or milling, so grinding matters if you want more than the fibre. A sudden fibre jump can upset digestion. Large amounts can bring bloating, fullness, or diarrhoea, so it makes sense to build up gradually. Normal servings are much smaller than 100 grams. A spoonful is useful, but it delivers only a fraction of this stat sheet in a real meal.
